docs.title: DevOps Notes
docs.text: A personal learning space for understanding DevOps — one concept, one command, and one problem at a time.

docs.title: About Me
docs.text:
Hi, I'm Prajjwal Saggar, a Computer Science student currently exploring and learning the world of DevOps, Linux, cloud infrastructure, containers, automation, and deployment.

I created this documentation as a place to learn by doing and document what I learn along the way.

These aren't meant to be perfect theoretical notes. They are my practical reference for the concepts, commands, problems, and workflows I encounter while learning DevOps.

docs.title: Why I Created This
docs.text:
DevOps can feel overwhelming when you first start.

You encounter things like:

Linux
  ↓
Networking
  ↓
Git
  ↓
Docker
  ↓
Kubernetes
  ↓
Cloud
  ↓
CI/CD
  ↓
Infrastructure

And suddenly there are hundreds of commands, tools, configuration files, and concepts to remember.

Instead of trying to memorize everything, I wanted to build something that I could come back to whenever I get stuck.

That's what this site is.

docs.title: For Anyone Starting DevOps
docs.text:
If you're also starting your DevOps journey, you can use these notes as a reference.

The goal isn't to learn every tool at once.

Start with the fundamentals:

Linux
  ↓
Networking
  ↓
Git
  ↓
Docker
  ↓
Cloud
  ↓
CI/CD
  ↓
Kubernetes

Understand why something works before worrying about memorizing the command.

For example, don't just memorize:

ssh -i key.pem ubuntu@server

Understand:

SSH
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Public / Private Keys
 ↓
~/.ssh/config
 ↓
Remote Server

Once the underlying concept makes sense, the commands become much easier to remember.

docs.title: Learning Philosophy
docs.text:
I don't want this to be a collection of commands that I memorize and forget.

The approach is:

Learn
  ↓
Understand
  ↓
Practice
  ↓
Break something
  ↓
Debug it
  ↓
Document it
  ↓
Understand it better

Most of the useful knowledge comes from the "why did this break?" part.

docs.title: DNS Cheat Sheet & DevOps Incident Workflow
DNS (Domain Name System)
docs.text:
DNS (Domain Name System) is the internet's phonebook. It translates human-friendly domain names such as:

learnlinux.tv

into numerical IP addresses such as:

172.105.29.178

This allows users to access websites using memorable domain names instead of IP addresses.

docs.title: Domain vs. Subdomain
docs.text:
Concept Description Example Domain The main website identity or primary address google.com Subdomain A specific section, service, or branch of a domain mail.google.com

For example:

mail.google.com
│    │      │
│    │      └── Top-level domain (TLD)
│    └───────── Domain
└────────────── Subdomain

docs.title: TTL (Time To Live)
docs.text:
TTL (Time To Live) specifies how long a DNS record can be cached before the DNS resolver should request a fresh copy.

TTL is measured in seconds.

For example:

TTL = 300

means the record can be cached for:

300 seconds = 5 minutes

A lower TTL allows DNS changes to propagate more quickly, while a higher TTL reduces the number of DNS queries.

docs.title: Port 53
docs.text:
DNS traditionally uses:

Port: 53

DNS queries primarily use UDP because it is fast and has low overhead.

DNS can also use TCP port 53, particularly for situations such as large responses or zone transfers.

docs.title: Authoritative
docs.text:
An authoritative DNS server is a server that holds the official DNS records for a domain.

Example:

example.com → 93.184.216.34

The authoritative server is responsible for providing the official answer for that domain.

docs.title: Non-Authoritative
docs.text:
A non-authoritative answer comes from a DNS resolver that obtained the information from another DNS server and may have it cached.

For example:

Your Computer
      ↓
Local DNS Resolver
      ↓
Authoritative DNS Server

The local resolver may return a cached answer without contacting the authoritative server every time.

docs.title: nslookup
docs.text: nslookup is a simple, cross-platform command-line tool used to perform DNS lookups.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
nslookup example.com

It can be used to quickly determine the IP address associated with a domain.

Example:

$ nslookup example.com

Name:    example.com
Address: 93.184.216.34

docs.title: dig
docs.text: dig is a more detailed DNS diagnostic tool commonly used on Linux and Unix-like systems.

docs.title: Basic Usage
docs.text:
dig example.com

It provides information such as:

  • DNS response status
  • Answer records
  • TTL values
  • Query execution time
  • DNS server used
  • Record types

Example structure:

;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NOERROR

;; QUESTION SECTION:
;example.com.       IN      A

;; ANSWER SECTION:
example.com.    300     IN      A       93.184.216.34

NOERROR indicates that the DNS query was successfully processed.

docs.title: Query a Specific DNS Server
docs.text:
You can explicitly specify which DNS resolver should answer your query.

For example, to query Google's public DNS:

dig @8.8.8.8 example.com

The syntax is:

dig @DNS_SERVER DOMAIN

For example:

dig @1.1.1.1 example.com

queries Cloudflare's DNS resolver.

This is useful when troubleshooting DNS because it allows you to compare responses from different resolvers.

docs.title: Common Public DNS Servers
docs.text: Provider IP Address Primary Feature Google Public DNS 8.8.8.8 / 8.8.4.4 Reliable global resolution Cloudflare DNS 1.1.1.1 / 1.0.0.1 Speed and privacy Quad9 DNS 9.9.9.9 Threat blocking

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
A website or microservice becomes unreachable after a:

  • Cloud server migration
  • Blue/Green deployment
  • Infrastructure change
  • DNS configuration change

The first thing to investigate is whether DNS is directing traffic to the correct server.

docs.title: Step 1: Identify the Traffic Destination
docs.text:
Run:

dig shop.company.com

Look at the ANSWER SECTION.

For example:

;; ANSWER SECTION:
shop.company.com.    300    IN    A    203.0.113.20

The returned IP address is:

203.0.113.20

Compare this IP with the IP address of the new server in your cloud provider or infrastructure platform.

For example:

DNS IP:          203.0.113.20
New Server IP:   203.0.113.20

If they match, DNS is pointing to the expected server.

docs.title: Step 2: Diagnose Caching vs. Misconfiguration
docs.text:
Query Google's public DNS directly:

dig @8.8.8.8 shop.company.com

Then compare it with your normal DNS lookup:

dig shop.company.com

docs.title: Case 1: Local DNS Shows OLD IP, Google Shows NEW IP
docs.text:
Example:

Local DNS:
shop.company.com → 203.0.113.10

Google DNS:
shop.company.com → 203.0.113.20

This suggests that the local resolver may still have the old DNS record cached.

Check the TTL:

dig shop.company.com

Look at the record:

shop.company.com.    120    IN    A    203.0.113.10

The TTL indicates how long the cached record may remain valid.

The old record should eventually expire, after which the resolver can retrieve the updated record.

docs.title: Case 2: Both Show the OLD IP
docs.text:
If both:

dig shop.company.com

and:

dig @8.8.8.8 shop.company.com

return the old IP, the problem is probably not just local caching.

Possible causes include:

  • DNS record was not updated
  • DNS provider configuration is incorrect
  • Wrong DNS zone was modified
  • Nameservers are pointing to a different DNS provider
  • The new record was created incorrectly

At this point, inspect the DNS configuration at the authoritative DNS provider.

docs.title: 4. DNS Migration Best Practice
docs.text:
Before performing a planned server migration or traffic cutover, reduce the DNS TTL.

For example:

Before migration:

TTL = 86400 seconds
       ↓
24 hours

Reduce it ahead of time:

TTL = 60 seconds

Then perform the migration or DNS cutover.

After the migration is stable, the TTL can be increased again.

docs.title: Typical Migration Flow
docs.text:
24+ hours before migration
        ↓
Lower DNS TTL
        ↓
Wait for old TTL to expire
        ↓
Migrate server
        ↓
Update DNS record
        ↓
Monitor traffic
        ↓
Verify DNS resolution
        ↓
Increase TTL again

The important point is that lowering the TTL immediately before changing the record does not instantly invalidate caches that were created under the previous TTL. The lower TTL should be configured sufficiently in advance.

docs.title: 5. Quick DNS Troubleshooting Cheat Sheet
docs.text: Goal Command Basic DNS lookup nslookup example.com Detailed DNS lookup dig example.com Query Google DNS dig @8.8.8.8 example.com Query Cloudflare DNS dig @1.1.1.1 example.com Query Quad9 DNS dig @9.9.9.9 example.com Check A record dig example.com A Check MX records dig example.com MX Check NS records dig example.com NS Check TXT records dig example.com TXT

docs.title: 6. Incident Decision Tree
docs.text:
Website unreachable
        │
        ▼
Run: dig shop.company.com
        │
        ▼
Is the returned IP correct?
       / \
     NO   YES
     │     │
     │     ▼
     │   Check server,
     │   firewall, ports,
     │   load balancer, etc.
     │
     ▼
Run:
dig @8.8.8.8 shop.company.com
        │
        ▼
Does Google DNS show the new IP?
       / \
     YES  NO
      │    │
      │    ▼
      │  Check DNS provider,
      │  authoritative records,
      │  nameservers, etc.
      │
      ▼
Likely caching/resolver
propagation issue

docs.title: 7. Key Takeaways
docs.text:
1. DNS translates domain names into IP addresses.
  2. TTL controls how long DNS responses can be cached.
  3. Port 53 is used for DNS, primarily over UDP, with TCP also used in certain cases.
  4. nslookup is useful for quick DNS checks.
  5. dig provides more detailed DNS troubleshooting information.
  6. dig @8.8.8.8 domain.com lets you query Google's public DNS directly.
  7. If different DNS resolvers return different IPs, caching or DNS propagation may be involved.
  8. If multiple independent resolvers return the old IP, investigate the authoritative DNS configuration.
  9. Lower DNS TTL well before a planned migration to make a future DNS cutover faster.
  10. DNS is only one part of troubleshooting an unreachable service; after confirming DNS, investigate networking, load balancers, firewalls, ports, and the application itself.

docs.title: SSH Keys & ~/.ssh/config — Vani's DevOps Story
docs.text: Scenario: Vani is a DevOps engineer. One laptop. Multiple GitHub accounts. Multiple servers. Multiple SSH keys. Her job is to make sure the right key goes to the right machine.

docs.title: 🚨 Day 1 — Vani Gets a Problem
docs.text:
Vani starts her new DevOps job.

Her setup looks like this:

Vani's Laptop
│
├── Personal GitHub
│
├── Work GitHub
│
├── AWS Production Server
│
└── Legacy Client Server

She tries to manage everything with one SSH key.

Very quickly, things become messy.

❌ Wrong GitHub account
❌ Wrong SSH key
❌ Permission denied
❌ Too many authentication failures
❌ "Why is GitHub using my personal account?!"

Her senior engineer tells her:

"Stop using one key for everything. Give every identity a proper key and let SSH decide which one to use."

That's where ssh-keygen and ~/.ssh/config come in.

docs.title: 🔑 1. First: What Exactly Is an SSH Key?
docs.text:
Vani runs:

ssh-keygen

SSH creates a key pair:

Private Key
     +
Public Key
     =
SSH Identity

Think of it like a lock-and-key system.

PUBLIC KEY
    ↓
The lock
Can be shared

PRIVATE KEY
    ↓
The actual key
Must stay with Vani

For example:

~/.ssh/id_ed25519
~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub

The first one is private.

The second one is public.

docs.title: Vani's golden rule
docs.text:
.pub       → Public → Safe to share
No .pub    → Private → NEVER share

docs.title: 🧠 2. How Does Vani Actually Log In?
docs.text:
Suppose Vani runs:

ssh ubuntu@server

The server doesn't receive her private key.

Instead, authentication roughly works like this:

             VANI'S LAPTOP
                  │
                  │
          "I want to log in"
                  │
                  ▼
          ┌───────────────┐
          │ Remote Server │
          └───────────────┘
                  │
                  │ Challenge
                  ▼
          Vani's SSH client
                  │
                  │ Uses PRIVATE KEY
                  ▼
          Cryptographic proof
                  │
                  ▼
          Remote server
                  │
                  │ Verifies using
                  │ PUBLIC KEY
                  ▼
             ✅ Access

The important part:

Vani's private key never needs to be sent to the server.

The server only needs her public key.

docs.title: 🔐 3. Vani Needs Four Different Identities
docs.text:
Now things get interesting.

Vani has:

1. Personal GitHub
2. Work GitHub
3. AWS Production
4. Legacy Client Server

Her senior says:

"Give each identity its own key."

So Vani creates:

~/.ssh/
├── work/
│   ├── github_work
│   └── aws_prod
│
└── personal/
    └── github_personal

But what about the legacy server?

It requires RSA.

So Vani creates:

legacy_server

Now she has different keys for different systems.

docs.title: ⚙️ 4. Choosing the Right Algorithm
docs.text:
Vani asks:

"What kind of key should I create?"

Her senior gives her this simple rule:

Situation Vani Uses Modern GitHub Ed25519 Modern Linux server Ed25519 AWS Ed25519 when supported Old/legacy system RSA 4096

So for modern systems:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519

For the legacy client:

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096

docs.title: Why Ed25519?
docs.text: It's modern, fast, compact, and widely supported.

docs.title: Why RSA 4096?
docs.text:
Because Vani's old client server doesn't support Ed25519.

So:

Modern system
      ↓
Ed25519

Legacy system
      ↓
RSA 4096

docs.title: 🛠️ 5. Vani Creates Her Work GitHub Key
docs.text:
Vani needs a separate identity for her company's GitHub.

She runs:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 \
  -f ~/.ssh/work/github_work \
  -C "vani@company.com"

SSH creates:

~/.ssh/work/
├── github_work
└── github_work.pub

She adds:

github_work.pub

to her work GitHub account.

The private key:

github_work

stays on her laptop.

docs.title: 🏠 6. Vani Creates Her Personal GitHub Key
docs.text:
Her personal GitHub needs a completely different identity.

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 \
  -f ~/.ssh/personal/github_personal \
  -C "vani@personal.com"

Now:

~/.ssh/
├── work/
│   └── github_work
│
└── personal/
    └── github_personal

She adds:

github_personal.pub

to her personal GitHub account.

Now her two GitHub identities are separated.

docs.title: ☁️ 7. Vani Gets Production Access
docs.text:
Her company has an AWS production server:

13.233.45.100

Vani creates another key:

ssh-keygen -t ed25519 \
  -f ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod \
  -C "vani@company.com"

Now:

~/.ssh/
├── work/
│   ├── github_work
│   └── aws_prod
│
└── personal/
    └── github_personal

She installs the corresponding public key on the production server.

docs.title: 🏚️ 8. Then Comes the Legacy Server...
docs.text:
Unfortunately, an old client server says:

"Ed25519? Never heard of it."

It requires RSA.

Vani doesn't argue.

She creates:

ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 \
  -f ~/.ssh/work/legacy_server \
  -C "vani@company.com"

Now she has:

~/.ssh/
├── work/
│   ├── github_work
│   ├── aws_prod
│   └── legacy_server
│
└── personal/
    └── github_personal

docs.title: 😵 9. Vani Has Too Many Keys
docs.text:
Now Vani has a new problem.

She could manually specify the key every time:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod ubuntu@13.233.45.100

But that's ugly.

And imagine doing this every day.

She wants to type:

ssh aws-prod

and have SSH automatically know:

"Oh, Vani means the AWS production server. Use aws_prod."

That's what:

~/.ssh/config

is for.

docs.title: 🧠 10. Vani Creates ~/.ssh/config
docs.text:
She runs:

nano ~/.ssh/config

And creates:

# Work GitHub
Host github-work
    HostName github.com
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work/github_work
    IdentitiesOnly yes

# Personal GitHub
Host github-personal
    HostName github.com
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/personal/github_personal
    IdentitiesOnly yes

# AWS Production
Host aws-prod
    HostName 13.233.45.100
    User ubuntu
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod
    IdentitiesOnly yes

# Legacy Client
Host legacy-client
    HostName legacy.example.com
    User admin
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work/legacy_server
    IdentitiesOnly yes

Now Vani has created aliases for her machines.

docs.title: 🏷️ 11. What Does Host Actually Mean?
docs.text:
This:

Host aws-prod

doesn't mean the actual server name.

It's simply Vani's nickname for the server.

So:

Host aws-prod
       ↓
Vani's nickname
       ↓
13.233.45.100

Now she can type:

ssh aws-prod

instead of:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod ubuntu@13.233.45.100

Much cleaner.

docs.title: 🗺️ 12. What Does HostName Mean?
docs.text:
This:

HostName 13.233.45.100

is the real destination.

So:

Host
  ↓
aws-prod

HostName
  ↓
13.233.45.100

Think:

Host     = Nickname
HostName = Actual address

docs.title: 👤 13. What Does User Mean?
docs.text:
Vani's AWS server expects the username:

ubuntu

So:

User ubuntu

For GitHub, SSH uses:

User git

That's why Git URLs look like:

git@github.com

The GitHub username isn't the SSH user.

The SSH user is simply:

git

docs.title: 🔑 14. What Does IdentityFile Mean?
docs.text:
This is the important one.

IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod

means:

"When Vani connects using this host, use this private key."

So:

ssh aws-prod
      │
      ▼
~/.ssh/config
      │
      ▼
Host aws-prod
      │
      ▼
IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod
      │
      ▼
Use AWS private key

docs.title: 🚧 15. Why Does Vani Need IdentitiesOnly yes?
docs.text:
Vani has many keys.

SSH might otherwise try several identities from her SSH agent.

That can result in errors such as:

Too many authentication failures

So she adds:

IdentitiesOnly yes

This tells SSH:

"For this host, don't randomly try every key I have. Use the identity I've configured."

docs.title: 🧪 16. Vani Tests Her AWS Connection
docs.text:
Instead of remembering:

ssh -i ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod ubuntu@13.233.45.100

she simply runs:

ssh aws-prod

SSH reads:

~/.ssh/config

and finds:

Host aws-prod
    HostName 13.233.45.100
    User ubuntu
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work/aws_prod

Result:

Vani
 │
 │ ssh aws-prod
 ▼
SSH Config
 │
 ├── HostName → 13.233.45.100
 ├── User → ubuntu
 └── Key → aws_prod
 │
 ▼
AWS Production

docs.title: 🐙 17. Now Vani Has a GitHub Problem
docs.text:
Vani runs:

git clone git@github.com:company/project.git

But which GitHub account should SSH use?

Her personal account?

Her work account?

SSH sees:

github.com

and doesn't know that Vani wants the work key.

This is where the Host aliases become extremely useful.

docs.title: 💼 18. Work GitHub
docs.text:
Vani configured:

Host github-work
    HostName github.com
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/work/github_work
    IdentitiesOnly yes

So instead of:

git clone git@github.com:company/project.git

she uses:

git clone git@github-work:company/project.git

Notice:

github-work

is NOT a real domain.

It's Vani's SSH alias.

SSH internally translates:

github-work
      ↓
github.com
      ↓
github_work private key

docs.title: 🏠 19. Personal GitHub
docs.text:
Her personal configuration is:

Host github-personal
    HostName github.com
    User git
    IdentityFile ~/.ssh/personal/github_personal
    IdentitiesOnly yes

So she clones personal repositories with:

git clone git@github-personal:vani-personal/project.git

Now:

git@github-work
        ↓
Work GitHub Key

git@github-personal
        ↓
Personal GitHub Key

Same physical domain:

github.com

Different SSH identities.

docs.title: 🧩 20. The Magic of ~/.ssh/config
docs.text:
Vani's entire setup can now be visualized like this:

                    ~/.ssh/config
                          │
          ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
          │               │                │
          ▼               ▼                ▼
    github-work    github-personal     aws-prod
          │               │                │
          ▼               ▼                ▼
     github.com       github.com      13.233.45.100
          │               │                │
          ▼               ▼                ▼
   github_work     github_personal     aws_prod
          │               │                │
          ▼               ▼                ▼
      Work GitHub    Personal GitHub    AWS Server

That's the entire purpose of SSH config:

Map a friendly alias to the correct destination, user, and private key.

docs.title: 🛠️ 21. Vani's Debugging Day
docs.text:
One morning:

ssh aws-prod

fails.

She wants to know what SSH is doing.

She runs:

ssh -v aws-prod

For even more detail:

ssh -vvv aws-prod

Now she can see:

Which config was loaded
Which host was selected
Which identity was attempted
Authentication methods
Server response

This is extremely useful when debugging SSH.

docs.title: 🔍 22. Vani Loses Her .pub File
docs.text:
One day she accidentally deletes:

github_work.pub

She panics.

But the private key still exists:

github_work

She can recreate the public key:

ssh-keygen -y \
  -f ~/.ssh/work/github_work \
  > ~/.ssh/work/github_work.pub

The private key remains the source of truth.

docs.title: 🆔 23. Vani Wants to Verify a Key
docs.text:
She can view the fingerprint:

ssh-keygen -l \
  -f ~/.ssh/work/github_work.pub

A fingerprint is a short representation of the key that can be used for verification.

docs.title: 🔒 24. Vani Protects Her Private Keys
docs.text:
She checks permissions:

ls -l ~/.ssh/work/github_work

Private keys should not be readable by everyone.

For example:

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/work/github_work

And remember:

❌ Never commit private keys
❌ Never upload private keys
❌ Never send private keys to someone
❌ Never put private keys in GitHub

Public keys are different:

✅ Public keys can be copied to servers
✅ Public keys can be added to GitHub

docs.title: Generate a modern key
docs.text: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/key_name

docs.title: Generate RSA 4096 for legacy systems
docs.text: ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -f ~/.ssh/key_name

docs.title: Change passphrase
docs.text: ssh-keygen -p -f ~/.ssh/key_name

docs.title: Recreate public key
docs.text: ssh-keygen -y -f ~/.ssh/key_name > ~/.ssh/key_name.pub

docs.title: Show fingerprint
docs.text: ssh-keygen -l -f ~/.ssh/key_name.pub

docs.title: Test SSH
docs.text: ssh alias-name

docs.title: Debug SSH
docs.text: ssh -v alias-name

docs.title: Edit SSH configuration
docs.text: nano ~/.ssh/config

docs.title: 🎯 26. Vani's Mental Model
docs.text:
Whenever Vani sees:

ssh something

she asks:

"What does 'something' mean?"
        │
        ▼
Check ~/.ssh/config
        │
        ▼
Find Host something
        │
        ▼
Where is HostName?
        │
        ▼
Which User?
        │
        ▼
Which IdentityFile?
        │
        ▼
Use that private key
        │
        ▼
Authenticate using public key
        │
        ▼
       ✅

And when she sees:

git clone git@github-work:company/project.git

she knows:

github-work
     ↓
SSH config alias
     ↓
github.com
     ↓
github_work private key
     ↓
Work GitHub account

docs.title: 🏆 The One Rule Vani Never Forgets
docs.text:
SSH
                     │
          ┌──────────┴──────────┐
          │                     │
       WHERE?                 WHO?
          │                     │
       HostName              User
          │                     │
          └──────────┬──────────┘
                     │
                  WHICH KEY?
                     │
                IdentityFile
                     │
                     ▼
              Correct Identity

ssh-keygen creates Vani's identities.

~/.ssh/config tells SSH which identity to use and where to use it.

That's the entire game.
